```python
def test_sort_array():

    assert sort_array([1, 5, 2, 3, 4]) == [1, 2, 4, 3, 5]

    # Includes zero (0 has zero 1-bits)
    assert sort_array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) == [0, 1, 2, 4, 3]

    # Descending input
    assert sort_array([7, 6, 5]) == [5, 6, 7]

    # Powers of two each have exactly one 1-bit, keep numeric order
    assert sort_array([8, 4, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 4, 8]

    # Negative numbers: bin(-n) contains '1' count of magnitude's bits
    # bin(-1) = '-0b1' -> 1 one-bit; bin(-2) = '-0b10' -> 1 one-bit
    assert sort_array([-2, -3, -4]) == [-2, -4, -3]

    # Empty array
    assert sort_array([]) == []

    # Single element
    assert sort_array([42]) == [42]

    # Duplicates preserved
    assert sort_array([3, 3, 1]) == [1, 3, 3]

    # Larger mixed case
    assert sort_array([2, 22, 10, 15, 7]) == [2, 10, 15, 7, 22]
```

```python
def test_sort_array():
    # Basic case: ties in bit-count preserve numeric order (stable sort)
    assert sort_array([1, 5, 2, 3, 4]) == [1, 2, 4, 3, 5]

    # Negative numbers: bin(x)[2:] uses magnitude bits
    assert sort_array([-2, -3, -4, -5, -6]) == [-4, -2, -6, -5, -3]

    # Includes zero (zero has zero '1' bits, comes first)
    assert sort_array([1, 0, 2, 3, 4]) == [0, 1, 2, 4, 3]

    # Edge cases: empty and single-element arrays
    assert sort_array([]) == []
    assert sort_array([7]) == [7]

    # Mixed values with differing bit counts
    assert sort_array([3, 6, 44, 12, 32, 5]) == [32, 3, 5, 6, 12, 44]

    # Powers of two all have exactly one '1' bit
    assert sort_array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32]) == [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]

    # Larger numbers
    assert sort_array([10, 100, 1000, 10000]) == [10, 100, 10000, 1000]

    # Descending input, increasing bit counts
    assert sort_array([15, 14, 13, 12]) == [12, 13, 14, 15]

    print("test_sort_array passed")
```
